 "evidenceSummary":"Two-group training intervention in 25 male semi-professional Australian footballers (13 Nordic hamstring, 12 isometric knee flexor hold) over 38 weeks, with matched periodised sprint training; allocation method is not described as randomized. Both groups increased biceps femoris long head fascicle length and eccentric strength, isometric strength fell in both groups, and the Nordic group had a 5 m split improvement and greater 40 m speed and maximal horizontal velocity than the isometric group at the end of pre-season.",
 "screeningLimitations":"There was no control group, so the effect of sprint training alone cannot be separated from the hamstring exercises, and the groups differed in age and baseline fascicle length. Fascicle length is estimated from an equation, and the sample is 25 athletes from one club, with no injury outcomes.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff may over-read the architecture and strength gains as proof of lower hamstring injury risk, when the study measured fascicle length and strength but did not measure injury incidence.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2023,
   "citation":"Timmins RG, Filopoulos D, Giannakis J, Nguyen V, Ruddy JD, Hickey JT, et al. The Impact of Eccentric or Isometric Training on Strength, Architecture, and Sprinting across an Australian Football Season. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2023 (published ahead of print).",
   "doi":"10.1249/MSS.0000000000003326",
   "abstract":"Twenty-five male semi-professional footballers completed 38 weeks of either Nordic hamstring or isometric knee flexor training alongside periodised sprinting. Both groups increased biceps femoris fascicle length and eccentric strength, isometric strength fell, and the Nordic group gained more sprint speed.",
   "tldr":"Nordic or isometric hamstring training combined with sprint training lengthened the biceps femoris and raised eccentric strength in footballers. Only the Nordic group improved short sprint times and maximal velocity, and isometric strength fell in both groups.",
   "methods":"An interventional cohort trial across pre-season and in-season with two allocated groups. Measures were ultrasound biceps femoris long head architecture, NordBord eccentric strength, force-plate isometric strength at 90/90, and a 40 m sprint with split times and force-velocity profiling. Training was matched for volume and time under tension (two sets of four 4-second repetitions), and linear mixed models assessed time and group effects.",
   "findings":"Both groups increased fascicle length from baseline (NHE 1.15 cm, ISO 0.81 cm, p<0.001 for each) and muscle thickness, and eccentric strength rose by 83 N in both groups from end of pre-season to end of the intervention. Isometric strength fell in both groups from baseline (NHE -45 N, ISO -80 N). The Nordic group improved its 5 m split within the group (-0.037 s), and at end of pre-season it had faster 40 m times (0.110 s) and higher maximal horizontal velocity (0.26 m/s) than the isometric group.",
   "limitations":"There was no control group, and the isometric group was older with a longer baseline fascicle length. The abstract reports the isometric fascicle gain as d=1.70 and the Nordic gain as 1.16 cm, while the results report d=0.81 and 1.15 cm, so the results values are used here. Injury incidence was not measured.",
   "practicalImplications":"An isometric hold alongside sprinting produced fascicle and eccentric gains in this squad, which may suit athletes who cannot tolerate Nordic soreness. Expect isometric strength to fall when tested in a different joint position from training, and use the Nordic option where short-sprint and maximal velocity gains are the goal.",
   "athleteDev":"Pair hamstring strength work with periodised sprinting, since sprint training may have contributed to the architecture gains, and choose the Nordic option where 5 m and maximal velocity improvement is the goal.",

METHODS
Participants
AC
 This interventional cohort trial was undertaken across the pre-season and in-season
period of the Victorian Football League (VFL) competition. The VFL is a second tier, semi-
professional ARF competition. Ethical approval for the study was granted by the Australian
Catholic University Human Research Ethics Committee (approval number: 2019-129E). All
athletes from a single VFL team were invited to participate and provide written, informed
consent. In total, 25 male athletes (age = 22±3yrs; height = 1.85±0.07m; body mass =
81.3±6.7kgs) were recruited and consented to participating.
 
 Study design
 Prior to the intervention commencing, all participants undertook a familiarisation session
with the NHE (Figure 1, Supplemental Video 1, Supplemental Digital Content 1), the
isometric knee flexion hold (ISO – Figure 1, Supplemental Video 2, Supplemental Digital
Content 2) and all testing methods. Following the familiarisation session (median = 5, range
5-7 days), all participants had the following baseline measures assessed:
 1. BFlh architecture;
 2. Maximal eccentric knee flexor strength during the NHE;
 3. Maximal isometric knee flexor strength with 90° of hip and knee flexion (90/90) (20);
 4. 40-metre sprint performance with splits at 5, 10, 20, 30 and 40-metres.
 a. With force-velocity profiles subsequently determined (21).
After these baseline assessments, participants were allocated into either the NHE group (n =
13) or the ISO group (n = 12). Participants in each intervention group only performed the one
hamstring-specific resistance training exercise for the entire pre-season and in-season period.
Additionally, all participants performed periodised sprinting as part of their on-field football
specific training sessions, with the prescribed intensity and volume matched between the
groups (Figure 2, Supplemental Tables 1a-1c, Supplemental Digital Content 3, The actual
versus planned weekly sprint distance (in metres), sprint efforts, and velocities undertaken at
≥25km/hr for the sprinting intervention, and The actual versus planned weekly sprint efforts
undertaken at ≥25km/hr for the sprinting intervention). All resistance and sprint training
sessions were undertaken with supervision from the members of research team, as part of
their roles in the strength and conditioning department of the football club (DF, VN, JG,
NMo). All participants undertook an initial six weeks of training after which there was a four
week break for the Christmas holiday period. Over these four weeks the participants were
 
 specifically instructed to refrain from resistance and sprint training. Following the holiday
period there was an additional eight weeks of training in the pre-season period (November to
March – total of 14 weeks – Figure 2). The subsequent in-season training period occurred
over the remaining 24 weeks between March and August.
 Architectural assessments of the BFlh using two-dimensional ultrasound were
completed at baseline and after 14 (end of pre-season) weeks as well as at the end of the
intervention (38 weeks). Both strength assessments (NHE and 90/90) were undertaken at
baseline, after 14 (end of pre-season) and 29 weeks as well as at the end of the intervention
(38 weeks). The maximal sprinting assessment was undertaken at baseline and after 14 weeks
of training (end of pre-season). During all on-field sessions (sprint training, football specific
and competitive matches), global positioning (GPS – OptimEye S5, 10Hz, Catapult Sports,
Melbourne, Australia) data were used to monitor the external load metrics of each group.
These metrics included: total distance covered, efforts undertaken at >25km/hr, distance
covered at >25km/hr, peak and average velocity of sprint efforts which were made relative to
each participant’s maximum recorded value.
A
Training intervention
 C As part of their weekly team resistance training sessions, all participants completed
one of either the NHE or ISO hold exercises. During the training intervention, all participants
also undertook a periodised sprint training intervention (Figure 2) prior to their on-field
football specific sessions. The frequency of both the sprinting and resistance training sessions
during the in-season period depended on the match schedule, with either one or two sessions
undertaken per week, with the sprinting and resistance training interventions matched
between the groups. When two sessions per week (both sprinting and resistance training)
 
 were undertaken, these were completed on non-consecutive days of the week (typically a
Tuesday and Thursday with a Saturday match). The training prescription was matched for the
NHE and ISO hold exercises across the entire intervention period and was two sets of four
repetitions (Table 1). Both the NHE and ISO hold exercise were undertaken for four second
repetitions to match total time under tension between the groups.
Nordic hamstring exercise training. A video of the NHE can be found in Supplemental
Video 1 (Supplemental Digital Content 1). Participants undertook the NHE with their ankles
secured underneath a fixed piece of gym equipment that allowed a standardised kneeling
height and position for all repetitions. This was preferred to the partner held version of the
NHE, where the strength of the partner may limit the effectiveness of the effort. For each
repetition, participants only performed the lowering (eccentric) portion of the NHE over a
four second period. After each repetition, participants were instructed to use their arms and
flex their hips to assist themselves in returning to the starting position, avoiding any
concentric contraction of the hamstrings. Once additional weight was utilised, the participants
were required to hold weight plates totalling 5, 7.5 or 10kg over their xiphoid process, per
previous work (REF). All NHE training was preceded by a warm up set of three submaximal,
bodyweight repetitions and following each training set participants were afforded a 2 min
rest. For all NHE training sessions across the intervention period, participants completed two
sets of four repetitions, which has previously been shown as an effective dose to maintain
eccentric knee flexor strength and BFlh fascicle lengths in recreational individuals (13).
Isometric hamstring training. A video of the ISO hold can be found in Supplemental Video
2 (Supplemental Digital Content 2). Participants started in a kneeling position, with their
ankles secured under a piece of gym equipment. The position was similar to the typical break
 
 point of the NHE, where their hips were slightly flexed, with a forward lean of approximately
45 degrees at the knee and using their arms to brace the upper body on a bench placed in
front of them. With the cues “hips under, quiet bum” participants were instructed to “pull up”
as hard and fast as they can against the fixed gym equipment for four seconds. Prior to each
training session participants undertook a sub-maximal warm up consisting of three ISO hold
repetitions at 50%, 75% and approximately 95% of their perceived maximum. Following
each training effort, participants were afforded a 30 second rest prior to the next attempt, with
two minutes rest between sets. For all ISO training sessions across the intervention period,
participants completed two sets of four repetitions, with training time matched between the
NHE and ISO groups.
 TE
Periodised sprint training. Prior to all on-field football specific training sessions, participants
undertook a periodised sprint intervention for the entire study period (Supplemental Tables 1a
– 1c, Supplemental Digital Content 3). All sprint training was preceded by an on-field group
warm up, following which participants undertook sub-maximal sprinting efforts prior to any
maximal attempts. For all the maximal efforts, participants were paired together based on
their maximal sprint velocity and undertook their efforts in a race format where they were
motivated to run faster than the person next to them. Across the study period, the number and
distance of the sprinting exposures was periodised to provide a progressive stimulus (Figure
2). This periodisation was planned on the assumption that the participants could potentially
not undertake any sprinting efforts during their football specific sessions or matches.
Therefore, should this occur, they will have still been exposed to a sprinting stimulus as part
of this prescription. During all sprint training efforts (≥25km/hr), velocity was collected
utilising GPS data (OptimEye S5, 10Hz, Catapult Sports, Melbourne, Australia) and recorded
as absolute and relative values. Relative velocity was determined as a percentage of each
 
 participant’s maximum recorded velocity, which was updated if it increased throughout the
study.
Outcome measures
BFlh architecture. The methods to assess BFlh architecture has been previously reported (5,
22, 23) Briefly, muscle thickness, pennation angle and fascicle len

completed at baseline and after 14 (end of pre-season) weeks as well as at the end of the
intervention (38 weeks). Both strength assessments (NHE and 90/90) were undertaken at
baseline, after 14 (end of pre-season) and 29 weeks as well as at the end of the intervention
(38 weeks). The maximal sprinting assessment was undertaken at baseline and after 14 weeks
of training (end of pre-season). During all on-field sessions (sprint training, football specific
and competitive matches), global positioning (GPS – OptimEye S5, 10Hz, Catapult Sports,
Melbourne, Australia) data were used to monitor the external load metrics of each group.
These metrics included: total distance covered, efforts undertaken at >25km/hr, distance
covered at >25km/hr, peak and average velocity of sprint efforts which were made relative to
each participant’s maximum recorded value.
A
Training intervention
 C As part of their weekly team resistance training sessions, all participants completed
one of either the NHE or ISO hold exercises. During the training intervention, all participants
also undertook a periodised sprint training intervention (Figure 2) prior to their on-field
football specific sessions. The frequency of both the sprinting and resistance training sessions
during the in-season period depended on the match schedule, with either one or two sessions
undertaken per week, with the sprinting and resistance training interventions matched
between the groups. When two sessions per week (both sprinting and resistance training)

NHE and ISO hold exercises across the entire intervention period and was two sets of four
repetitions (Table 1). Both the NHE and ISO hold exercise were undertaken for four second
repetitions to match total time under tension between the groups.

Video 1 (Supplemental Digital Content 1). Participants undertook the NHE with their ankles

NHE, where the strength of the partner may limit the effectiveness of the effort. For each

four second period. After each repetition, participants were instructed to use their arms and
flex their hips to assist themselves in returning to the starting position, avoiding any
concentric contraction of the hamstrings. Once additional weight was utilised, the participants

sets of four repetitions, which has previously been shown as an effective dose to maintain

ankles secured under a piece of gym equipment. The position was similar to the typical break

45 degrees at the knee and using their arms to brace the upper body on a bench placed in

participants completed two sets of four repetitions, with training time matched between the
NHE and ISO groups.

maximal attempts. For all the maximal efforts, participants were paired together based on

motivated to run faster than the person next to them. Across the study period, the number and
distance of the sprinting exposures was periodised to provide a progressive stimulus (Figure

not undertake any sprinting efforts during their football specific sessions or matches.

study.

content.content:
RESULTS
Participant details and intervention compliance
 The two groups were similar with respect to height and body mass (NHE height
183±8cm, body mass 79.5±7.2kg; ISO height 185±6cm, body mass 83.4±5.6kg; height
p=0.445, body mass p=0.152). However, on average the ISO group (24±3 years) were older
than the NHE cohort (21±2 years; p=0.02). Of the 76 total resistance training sessions, the
NHE group had an average compliance of 81±15% (range: 41 to 76 sessions completed). The
ISO group had a similar level of compliance with 78±14% (range: 40 to 76 sessions
completed).
External load metrics
 There were no significant differences between the groups, at any of the weeks
throughout the intervention when comparing the number of weekly sprinting efforts (p range
across all weeks = 0.231 to 0.982) and distance covered ≥25km/hr (p range across all weeks
= 0.203 to 0.986), as well as the average relative velocity of these sprinting efforts ≥25km/hr
(p range across all weeks = 0.161 to 0.998).
BFlh architectural characteristics
 A summary of the BFlh architectural variables during this intervention can be found
in Figure 3 and Supplemental Table 2a (Supplemental Digital Content 3).
Fascicle length. There was a significant main effect for time (p<0.001), but not for group
(p=0.081) on BFlh fascicle length. Both the NHE and ISO groups had a significant increase
 
 in fascicle length from baseline to the end of pre-season (NHE group: difference 0.73cm,
95% CI 0.53 to 0.94cm, d = 1.33, p < 0.001; ISO group: difference 0.51cm, 95% CI 0.34 to
0.67cm, d = 0.92, p < 0.001). At the end of the intervention, both groups saw a further
significant increase in fascicle length compared to the end of pre-season (NHE group:
difference 0.42cm, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.88cm, d = 0.68, p = 0.038; ISO group: difference
0.31cm, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.57cm, d = 0.59, p = 0.021). These changes were also significantly
increased when compared to baseline measures for both groups (NHE group: difference
1.15cm, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.63cm, d = 1.88, p < 0.001; ISO group: difference 0.81cm, 95% CI
0.58 to 1.06cm, d = 0.81, p < 0.001). The NHE group had significantly shorter fascicles than
the ISO group at baseline (difference 0.57cm, 95% CI 0.13 to 1.01cm, d = 1.07, p = 0.013),
but there were no differences at the other time points (d range: 0.39 to 0.59, p range: 0.151 to
0.322).
Muscle thickness. BFlh muscle thickness showed a significant main effect for group
(p=0.013) and time (p<0.001). Post hoc analysis indicated that both groups demonstrated a
significant increase in muscle thickness from baseline to the end of the intervention (NHE:
difference 0.11cm, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.21cm, d = 0.51, p = 0.032; ISO: difference 0.21cm, 95%
CI 0.10 to 0.32cm, d = 0.86, p = 0.002). However, only the ISO group demonstrated a
significant increase when compared to the end of pre-season (difference 0.13cm, 95% CI 0.01
to 0.25cm, d = 0.52, p = 0.048), whereas the NHE group did not (difference 0.03cm, 95% CI
-0.03 to 0.11cm, d = 0.19, p = 0.332). Between-group comparisons showed that the ISO
group had a significantly thicker muscle than the NHE group at the end of the intervention
(difference 0.26cm, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.42cm, d = 1.37, p = 0.002), but there were no
differences at other time points.
 
 Pennation angle. There were no significant main effects for group (p=0.188) or time
(p=0.471) found for BFlh pennation angle. Therefore, no post hoc analyses were undertaken.
Eccentric knee flexor strength
 A significant main effect for time (p<0.001), but not group (p=0.503) was found for
eccentric knee flexor strength. Post hoc analyses showed a significant increase in eccentric
knee flexor strength at the end of the intervention when compared to the end of pre-season for
both groups (NHE: 83N, 95% CI 53 to 114N, d = 1.79, p < 0.001; ISO: 83N, 95% CI 17 to
151N, d = 1.17, p = 0.018; Figure 4 and Supplemental Table 2b, Supplemental Digital
Content 3). There were no differences between groups at any time point (d range = 0.02 to
0.35, p range = 0.384 to 0.940).
Isometric knee flexor strength
 A significant main effect for time (p<0.001), but not group (p=0.340) was found for
isometric knee flexor strength. Post hoc analyses showed a significant decrease in isometric
knee flexor strength from baseline to the end of pre-season for both groups (NHE: -28N,
95%CI -51 to -5N, d = -0.58, p = 0.020; ISO: -39N, 95% CI -65 to -13N, d = -1.10, p <
0.001; Figure 4 and Supplemental Table 2b, Supplemental Digital Content 3). These
reductions persisted through the intervention for both groups (NHE: -45N, 95% CI -81 to -
8N, d = -1.03, p = 0.022; ISO: -80N, 95% CI -104 to -56N, d = -3.35, p < 0.001), with only
the ISO group getting weaker during the in-season period (difference in NHE: -16N, 95% CI
-46 to 16N, d = -0.47, p = 0.268; difference in ISO: -41N, 95% CI -74 to -8N, d = -1.18, p =
0.019). The NHE group was stronger isometrically than the ISO group at the end of the
intervention (difference 29N, 95% CI 9 to 49N, d = 1.20, p = 0.006).
 
 Sprint assessment
Split results. A significant main effect for time (p=0.003), but not group (p=0.619) was found
for 5m split times. Post hoc analyses showed a significant decrease in 5m split times (i.e.,
improved performance) from baseline to the end of the pre-season period in the NHE group
only (NHE: -0.037s, 95% CI -0.681 to -0.014s, d = -0.83, p = 0.043; ISO: -0.021N, 95% CI -
0.693 to 0.010, d = -0.82, p = 0.056; Figure 5 and Supplemental Table 2c, Supplemental
Digital Content 3). There were no differences in 5m split times at any time point when
comparing between the groups (d range = -0.07 to 0.72 and p range = 0.102 to 0.876).
 A significant main effect for group (p=0.009) and time (p=0.023) was also found for
40m sprint performance. Post hoc analyses found that the NHE group was significantly faster
over 40m when compared to the ISO group at the end of pre-season (Difference 0.110s, 95%
CI 0.006 to 0.214s, d = 0.87, p = 0.039). There were no other significant within or between
group changes in 40m sprint performance (d range = 0.03 to 0.72, p range = 0.085 to 0.993).
A
Horizontal force-velocity profile. A significant main effect for group (p=0.007) and time
(p=0.021) was found for maximal horizontal velocity. Post hoc analyses found that the NHE
group had a significantly greater horizontal velocity than the ISO group at the end of pre-
season (Difference 0.26m/s, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.51m/s, d = 0.82, p = 0.049; Supplemental
Table 3, Supplemental Digital Content 3). There were no other significant within or between
group changes in horizontal force-velocity profiles (d range = 0.06 to 0.82, p range = 0.057 to
0.876)
 
 DISCUSSION
 This is the first study to investigate the impact of a long-term (38 week) NHE or isometric
knee flexor training intervention, alongside a periodised sprinting program, on BFlh
architecture, strength and sprinting performance in ARF athletes. The novel findings of this
study are:
 1. Undertaking a NHE or isometric knee flexor training intervention, alongside a
 periodised sprinting program, significantly improves BFlh fascicle length and muscle
 thickness across 38 weeks.
 2. Both interventions also significantly increase eccentric strength across the in-season
 period, with no alterations during pre-season.
 3. Isometric knee flexor strength significantly reduced at the end of both the pre-season
 for both groups, with the ISO group getting weaker in-season.
 4. Undertaking NHE training, alongside a periodised sprinting program, across a 14
 week pre-season period can significantly improve 5m split time, and
 5. A NHE intervention, alongside a periodised sprinting program, can significantly
 improve maximal sprinting velocity over 40m when compared to an ISO training
 intervention after a 14 week pre-season period.
 This is the first study to prescribe a single-mode hamstring specific exercise intervention,
alongside a periodised sprinting program, in semi-professional co

d['evidenceSummary']="Systematic review and robust variance estimation meta-analysis of 10 studies (211 participants, mostly male) comparing high and low body fat groups during aerobic exercise in the heat, from 1,222 screened records. d['screeningLimitations']="Participants were mostly physically inactive (70%), unacclimatized children and adults under 30 rather than athletes, and post-exercise core temperature never exceeded 38°C. p['limitations']="Participants were mostly physically inactive (70%) children and adults under 30, and post-exercise core temperature stayed below 38°C, so the results do not cover hyperthermic conditions. The abstract gives the low body fat group as 17.8% while the results give 17.69%."
p['practicalImplications']="This review cannot show whether body fat on its own raises heat strain, because the pooled comparisons were null, underpowered and limited to core temperatures below 38°C. The one study that matched groups for body mass and surface area found higher core temperature in the high body fat group, so higher body fat should not be treated as harmless in the heat."
p['athleteDev']="The pooled data cannot guide heat-training adjustments by body fat percentage. One included study found that obese boys acclimatized to heat more slowly than lean boys, but this was not tested in athletes."

 "evidenceSummary: said no differences 'among the 18 interventions' -> pooled estimates came only from interventions with unbiased comparisons ('Only studies that allowed for unbias comparisons were included in the RVE model')",

 "practicalImplications: advice to monitor body mass, surface area and acclimatization alongside body composition was not a finding (the paper's practical implications address research design only) -> states what the evidence cannot show and the one controlled study's higher core temperature in Hi-BF (Dervis et al.)",
 "athleteDev: generic heat-planning advice -> limited to what the review reports (obese boys 'acclimatized at a slower rate')"
],"Exertional heat illness context; journal pre-proof with no volume or pages, year 2021 taken from the 'Please cite' line.",'high')

],"Fatigue index direction is described inconsistently in the paper (abstract 'decrease in fatigue index', discussion 'FI increased by 2.5% in favor of napping'). Year 2023 is from the online-first copyright line; no issue citation printed.",'normal')

p['athleteDev']="The most actionable point for performance staff is timing: evening caffeine above about 2 mg/kg before training or competition was linked to shorter, less efficient sleep, so screen and adjust caffeine use around evening sessions."
save(d,"CORRECTED",[
 "screeningLimitations: 'often under 20 participants' is not stated -> '21 randomized control trials, a total of 314 participants'; 'several used unvalidated subjective tools' made specific (seven studies)",

 "athleteDev: removed 'plan extra sleep opportunities the next day after any night of poor sleep', which the review does not study"
],"",'normal')

d=load('Q95'); p=d['paper']
d['screeningLimitations']="Data came from one team, one coaching staff and four weeks of sessions, and warm-up type was set by the coaches and tied to match-day position (Reaction Speed the day before a match, Speed two days before, Run the day after), so differences may reflect session context as well as the warm-up. Intensity bands were relative to each player's mesocycle maximum, and the authors caution against extrapolating to other squads."
p['practicalImplications']="The authors suggest matching the warm-up to the work that follows: Reaction Speed before technical-tactical sessions, Speed before high-intensity sessions and Run before longer or moderate sessions, and avoiding Speed warm-ups close to competition.  "practicalImplications: recommended a 25 to 90 minute nap, which the paper does not state, and said longer gaps were 'linked to less fatigue' -> the meta-regression found no effect of nap duration (p = 0.39) and linked a longer nap-to-exercise gap to a larger fatigue index (performance decrement) benefit, not perceived fatigue (coefficient 0.01, p = 0.04)",
 "athleteDev: removed the unsupported 25 to 90 minute range and added that other performance outcomes are not established"
],"Fatigue index direction is described inconsistently in the paper (abstract 'decrease in fatigue index', discussion 'FI increased by 2.5% in favor of napping'). Year 2023 is from the online-first copyright line; no issue citation printed.",'normal')

d=load('Q94'); p=d['paper']
d['screeningLimitations']="Only 16 of 35 studies measured sleep objectively, the 21 randomized trials recruited 314 participants in total, and females were underrepresented, which limits generalization across sexes and sports. Many studies gave limited detail on dietary control and attrition, and seven studies with only subjective outcomes did not use validated sleep tools."
p['limitations']="Only 61% of studies were randomized trials, and females made up 26% (82 of 314) of randomized trial participants in the results, which the limitations section rounds to 20%, so causality and generalization are limited. The abstract's claim about tryptophan-rich protein is stronger than the body-text results, where three of four studies found no sleep change."
p['athleteDev']="The most actionable point for performance staff is timing: evening caffeine above about 2 mg/kg before training or competition was linked to shorter, less efficient sleep, so screen and adjust caffeine use around evening sessions."
save(d,"CORRECTED",[
 "screeningLimitations: 'often under 20 participants' is not stated -> '21 randomized control trials, a total of 314 participants'; 'several used unvalidated subjective tools' made specific (seven studies)",
 "limitations: females 'about 20%' of trial participants -> 26% (n = 82) per results ('only 26% (n = 82) of these being female'), noting the limitations section says 20%",
 "athleteDev: removed 'plan extra sleep opportunities the next day after any night of poor sleep', which the review does not study"
],"",'normal')

d=load('Q95'); p=d['paper']
d['screeningLimitations']="Data came from one team, one coaching staff and four weeks of sessions, and warm-up type was set by the coaches and tied to match-day position (Reaction Speed the day before a match, Speed two days before, Run the day after), so differences may reflect session context as well as the warm-up. Intensity bands were relative to each player's mesocycle maximum, and the authors caution against extrapolating to other squads."
p['practicalImplications']="The authors suggest matching the warm-up to the work that follows: Reaction Speed before technical-tactical sessions, Speed before high-intensity sessions and Run before longer or moderate sessions, and avoiding Speed warm-ups close to competition. These are untested recommendations, but monitoring the starting speed of repeated efforts follows from its strong effect on acceleration and deceleration counts."
save(d,"CORRECTED",[
 "screeningLimitations: added that warm-up type was confounded with days from the match ('performed during sessions the day before the match' / 'the day after the match' / '2 days before the match')",
 "practicalImplications: framed the session-matching advice as the authors' untested suggestion rather than a finding"
],"Players are described only as 'highly trained' U23 league players with sex not stated; coded Professional / Elite as in the draft, which a reviewer may prefer to change.",'normal')

d=load('Q96'); p=d['paper']
d['evidenceSummary']="Two-group training intervention in 25 male semi-professional Australian footballers (13 Nordic hamstring, 12 isometric knee flexor hold) over 38 weeks, with matched periodised sprint training; allocation method is not described as randomized. Both groups increased biceps femoris long head fascicle length and eccentric strength, and isometric strength fell in both groups. At the end of pre-season the Nordic group had a within-group 5 m split improvement (the isometric group's similar change was p = 0.056) and was faster over 40 m with higher maximal horizontal velocity than the isometric group, without a within-group 40 m change."
p['tldr']="Nordic or isometric hamstring training combined with sprint training lengthened the biceps femoris and raised eccentric strength in footballers, while isometric strength fell in both groups. Sprint differences favouring the Nordic group were small and limited to the end of pre-season."
p['practicalImplications']="Either hamstring exercise, paired with periodised sprinting, was followed by fascicle length and eccentric strength gains in this squad, so the isometric hold is a workable alternative where the Nordic is not used. The fall in 90/90 isometric strength may reflect joint angle or contraction mode specificity, so interpret that test cautiously during such programs."
p['athleteDev']="Pair hamstring strength work with periodised sprinting. The Nordic group's sprint advantage was a between-group difference at end of pre-season with no within-group 40 m change, so it is not strong evidence that the Nordic improves sprint speed more than the isometric hold."
save(d,"CORRECTED",[
 "tldr: 'Only the Nordic group improved short sprint times and maximal velocity' -> maximal velocity and 40 m were between-group differences only ('There were no other significant within or between group changes in 40m'); the isometric 5 m change was d = -0.82, p = 0.056 vs Nordic d = -0.83, p = 0.043, with no between-group 5 m difference",
 "practicalImplications: 'may suit athletes who cannot tolerate Nordic soreness' (soreness not measured) and 'use the Nordic option where short-sprint and maximal velocity gains are the goal' -> removed; isometric strength loss framed as the authors' joint angle or contraction mode explanation",
 "athleteDev: removed recommendation to choose the Nordic for 5 m and maximal velocity gains",
 "evidenceSummary: clarified within-group vs between-group sprint findings"
],"Semi-professional (VFL second tier) players coded Professional / Elite. Published ahead of print; year 2023 from the copyright line, no volume or pages printed.",'high')
